fmt_yr <- function (arg0_y) {

# Abstract

The classical epoch of South Asia, spanning from the accession of Chandragupta I in 319AD to the rise of regional mediaeval kingdoms around 750AD, represents a transformative phase in the subcontinent's demographic and agrarian history. Across a vast territory of 3,94M km² (encompassing 3.938.787 km² and 51.246 active terrestrial grid cells), human settlement integrated the imperial heartlands of the middle and lower Ganga with the fertile alluvial deltas of Bengal and Assam, the semi-arid maritime littoral of Gujarat and Saurashtra, the river valleys of the Indus and Punjab, and the volcanic black-cotton plateaux of the Vakataka Deccan. Far from witnessing systemic demographic retrenchment, the era was defined by expansive rural colonisation, royal copper-plate land grants (*shasanas* and *agrahara* endowments), sophisticated hydraulic engineering and resilient agrarian communities that accommodated fluctuating monsoonal regimes.

Under the INDUS regional reconstruction, macro-regional population grew from 52,00M inhabitants in 319AD to 56,50M in 400AD, climbing to 59,00M in 500AD at the height of Imperial Gupta hegemony. Following sixth-century Huna disruptions, the fragmentation of central authority and the subsequent political consolidation under Harsha of Kannauj (606AD to 647AD) and contemporary regional dynasties (Maitrakas of Valabhi, Gauda rulers, Kamarupa kings and Later Guptas), population advanced steadily to 61,00M in 600AD, 62,50M in 650AD and reached 64,00M by 750AD. Aggregate population density increased from 13,20 persons per km² in 319AD to 16,25 persons per km² in 750AD.

Demographic mass remained anchored in the Gangetic plain and eastern riverine deltas. By 750AD, the Madhyadesha and Magadha core (21,76M inhabitants, 34,00% of subcontinental total) and the Gauda, Bengal and Kamarupa macro-province (14,08M, 22,00%) concentrated more than 55% of all inhabitants on just 27,76% of the land area. The Madhyadesha core achieved the highest provincial density at 47,06 persons per km², sustained by perennial Himalayan snow-melt tributaries, intensive double-cropping of rice and wheat, and ancient urban hubs such as Patna, Kannauj, Varanasi and Mathura. In contrast, the extensive western and north-western provinces of Malwa and Gujarat (12,80M, 13,13 persons per km²), Punjab, Kashmir and Sindh (8,32M, 7,61 persons per km²), and the Vakataka Deccan (7,04M, 9,06 persons per km²) sustained lower aggregate densities, though punctuated by prominent commercial emporia and royal citadels including Ujjain, Valabhi, Bharuch, Peshawar, Thanesar, Multan and Kanchipuram.

This study reconstructs the historical demography of classical South Asia by coupling 12.898 georeferenced settlement trajectories ($\alpha = 0,87$, $R^2 = 0,96$) with comprehensive epigraphic inventories of copper-plate land grants, archaeological surveys of habitation mounds, primary-monograph urban series, palaeoclimatic speleothem records and classical travelogues, notably those of Faxian and Xuanzang [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making]. By evaluating settlement subtraction against archaeological reality, the reconstruction demonstrates that urban transformation during the mid-first millennium AD represented functional decentralisation and rural agrarian intensification rather than continental demographic collapse.

# Political Architecture and Regional Sub-Divisions

## Imperial Guptas and the Madhyadesha Core

The political landscape of northern and central South Asia was reshaped during the fourth century AD by the rise of the Imperial Gupta dynasty from its ancestral base in eastern Uttar Pradesh and Magadha [@neill2020empires; @mishra2026historical]. Chandragupta I (c. 319AD to 335AD) established imperial sovereignty, forming an alliance with the Lichchhavis and assuming the title of *Maharajadhiraja*. His successor, Samudragupta (c. 335AD to 375AD), recorded his extensive military campaigns on the famous Prayaga stone pillar inscription composed by his court poet Harishena. The inscription delineates a multi-tiered imperial structure: direct annexation of the rulers of Aryavarta in the Gangetic basin, subjugation and tributary subordination of forest kingdoms (*atavika rajyas*) in central India, and tributary recognition from frontier potentates in Kamarupa, Samatata, Kartripura and Licchavi Nepal [@neill2020empires; @dwivedi2021tools; @Slusser1982NepalMandala; @Phuntsho2013HistoryBhutan].

Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (c. 375AD to 415AD) extended Gupta authority to the Arabian Sea by subjugating the Western Kshatrapas (Sakas) in Malwa and Saurashtra, securing control over lucrative maritime trade conduits operating through Bharuch, Cambay and Sopara [@seland2014archaeolog; @sheikh2004state]. Dynastic matrimonial alliances cemented this vast sphere: Prabhavatigupta, daughter of Chandragupta II, married Rudrasena II of the Deccan Vakataka dynasty, eventually ruling as regent over Vidarbha and coordinating northern and southern political spheres [@neill2020empires; @policardi2024goddess]. Under Kumaragupta I (c. 415AD to 455AD), the founding of Nalanda Mahavihara marked the pinnacle of state patronage for higher learning and monastic organisation [@shaw2013archaeolog; @verardi2018gods].

By the late fifth century AD, incursions by the Alkhan Hunas under Toramana and Mihirakula fractured imperial control in the north-west and Punjab [@morris2019central; @verardi2012buddhism]. Skandagupta (c. 455AD to 467AD) mounted successful defensive campaigns, recorded in the Bhitari pillar inscription and the Junagadh rock inscription commemorating the repair of the Sudarshana lake embankment [@singh2020hydrology]. Nevertheless, succession disputes, economic realignments and the rise of ambitious feudatories (*samantas*) led to political devolution. In the sixth and seventh centuries, regional powers emerged: the Maitrakas of Valabhi in Saurashtra, the Pushyabhutis of Thanesar and Kannauj under Prabhakaravardhana and Harsha, the Later Guptas of Magadha and Malwa, Shashanka of Gauda in Bengal, and the Varman dynasty in Kamarupa [@targa1999pala; @kovacs2024bengal; @sharma2011empire].

## Territorial Organisation and Administrative Hierarchy

Imperial governance across classical South Asia operated through an articulated hierarchical administrative geography that balanced centralised royal oversight with corporate local self-governance [@neill2020empires; @mishra2026historical]. At the apex of provincial administration stood the province, designated as a *desha*, *rashtra* or *bhukti*, governed by a royal prince (*kumaramatya*) or an imperial viceroy titled *uparika* or *uparikamahadanda-nayaka* [@neill2020empires]. Prominent examples include Pundravardhana bhukti in North Bengal, Tirabhukti in North Bihar, and Saurashtra rashtra in western India.

Each *bhukti* was partitioned into administrative districts termed *vishayas*, supervised by a district magistrate (*vishayapati*) whose headquarters (*adhishthana*) coordinated regional tax collection, judicial administration and police defense [@kovacs2024bengal; @dwivedi2021tools]. The *vishayas* were subdivided into sub-districts known as *vithis*, which comprised clusters of agricultural villages termed *gramas*. At the village level, administration was conducted by the headman (*gramika*) or village elders (*mahattaras*), collaborating with the local council (*panchamandali*) to maintain boundary records, settle property disputes and apportion shared obligations for maintaining irrigation canals, tanks and protective embankments [@singh2020hydrology; @targa1999pala].

The coordination between royal officials and local agrarian leaders ensured that tax obligations (*bhaga*, *kara* and *bali*) were assessed according to seasonal crop yields rather than arbitrary quotas. Village assemblies preserved records of land ownership, irrigation rights and communal pastures on cloth or palm-leaf scrolls (*pustakas*), which were verified by village accountants (*pustapalas*) before any property transfer could be inscribed on copper plates [@neill2020empires; @dwivedi2021tools].

## Numismatic Evidence and Currency Spheres

Numismatic discoveries provide critical insights into imperial fiscal capacity, trade connections and metallic standards across the classical era [@dwivedi2021tools; @neill2020empires]. The Imperial Guptas minted magnificent series of gold coins (*dinaras*), initially struck on the Kushan weight standard of approximately 120 to 123 grains (7,8 to 8,0 grams) and later reformed by Skandagupta to the national Indian *suvarna* standard of 144 grains (9,3 grams) [@dwivedi2021tools]. Obverse types, including the Archer, Lion-Slayer, Tiger-Slayer, Horseman and Asvamedha types, celebrated imperial paramountcy and martial prowess, while the reverse consistently featured the goddess Lakshmi or Ganga [@policardi2024goddess].

Following the annexation of western India by Chandragupta II, the empire introduced silver currency modelled directly on the drachms of the Western Kshatrapas [@sheikh2004state]. These silver issues, weighing approximately 30 to 34 grains, met the monetary requirements of western commercial trade across Gujarat and Malwa. Copper coinages were issued in limited quantities, primarily in the Malwa and Mathura sectors [@khattak2025major]. For everyday market transactions, low-value agricultural exchanges and rural bazaar commerce, cowrie shells (*kapardaka*) functioned as the primary currency, as explicitly observed by Faxian during his fifth-century travels through Madhyadesha [@dwivedi2021tools]. The persistence of cowries, gold dinaras and silver drammas demonstrates that monetisation remained adapted to distinct commercial tiers rather than suffering sudden demonetisation.

## Five Macro-Provinces

INDUS partitions classical South Asia into five physiographically and politically coherent macro-provinces bounded by mountain ranges, major river divides and climatic boundaries (Table \ref{tab:subregions}):

### Madhyadesha, Magadha and Prayaga-Kannauj Core

The Madhyadesha and Magadha core (462.384 km², 11,74% of the regional domain) forms the imperial axis of northern India, spanning the fertile doabs between the Yamuna and Ganga rivers eastward into the Magadhan plain of southern Bihar. Encompassing 2.484 catalogued settlements and celebrated classical cities including Pataliputra (Patna), Kanyakubja (Kannauj), Varanasi, Mathura, Ayodhya, Kaushambi, Shravasti and Rajgir, this province sustained the densest rural population in the subcontinent [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @hawkes2020back; @khattak2025major]. By 319AD, its population stood at 17,68M (38,24 persons per km²), rising to 19,21M in 400AD, 20,06M in 500AD and reaching 21,76M by 750AD (47,06 persons per km²). The province concentrated 34,00% of the entire macro-regional population on less than one-eighth of its land.

Beyond its agrarian primacy, the province functioned as the ideological and ritual nucleus of the empire. The sacred confluence of the Ganga and Yamuna at Prayaga served as the setting for royal redistributive assemblies, culminating in the quinquennial assemblies convened by Harsha where royal treasuries were systematically distributed to religious figures, scholars and the indigent [@targa1999pala; @verardi2018gods].

### Gauda, Pundravardhana, Samatata and Kamarupa

Spanning Bengal and the Brahmaputra valley of Assam (631.135 km², 16,02%), this province encompasses the humid lower deltas of the Ganga, Brahmaputra and Meghna river systems and 2.744 catalogued settlements [@kovacs2024bengal; @sharma2011empire; @Eaton1993Rise]. Supported by abundant rainfall, perennial inundation and deltaic sedimentation, agricultural colonisation expanded rapidly across active deltaic tracts. Epigraphic records document extensive land grants across Pundravardhana (North Bengal), Vanga (Southern Bengal), Samatata (Eastern Bengal delta) and Kamarupa [@targa1999pala]. Major regional centres included Gaur (Lakshmanavati), Mahasthangarh (Pundranagara), Tamralipti, Chandraketugarh, Karnasuvarna and Pragjyotishpura (Guwahati). Population expanded from 11,44M in 319AD to 12,98M in 500AD and reached 14,08M by 750AD (22,31 persons per km²).

### Malwa, Ujjain, Maitraka Valabhi and Western Provinces

Covering 975.022 km² (24,75% of regional area) with 2.165 catalogued settlements, this expansive western province encompasses the fertile black-cotton Malwa plateau, the Vindhyan scarplands, the Gulf of Khambhat and the semi-arid peninsulas of Gujarat and Saurashtra [@sheikh2004state; @kumar2025investigat]. Ujjain served as a primary political and astronomical hub, while Valabhi functioned as the capital of the Maitraka dynasty and an internationally renowned centre of Buddhist scholarship [@verardi2018gods]. Ports such as Bharuch (Bhrigukachchha), Cambay and Patan connected overland caravan routes with Indian Ocean maritime networks [@seland2014archaeolog; @cobb2018black]. The provincial population rose from 10,40M in 319AD to 11,80M in 500AD and reached 12,80M by 750AD (13,13 persons per km²).

### Punjab, Thanesar, Kashmir and North-Western Frontier

The north-western province (1.093.083 km², 27,75%) encompasses 2.411 catalogued settlements across the five rivers of the Punjab basin, the Vale of Kashmir, the Potohar plateau, the middle and lower Indus valley of Sindh, and the frontier corridors linking South Asia with Central Asia [@petrie2017adaptation; @morris2019central; @verardi2012buddhism]. Thanesar (Sthanvishvara) served as the ancestral base of the Pushyabhuti dynasty before Harsha transferred his capital to Kannauj. Other prominent centres included Peshawar (Purushapura), Taxila, Multan, Srinagar, Delhi, Mansura, Alor, Sialkot (Sakala) and Lahore. Population climbed from 6,76M in 319AD to 7,67M in 500AD and reached 8,32M by 750AD (7,61 persons per km²), reflecting lower agricultural carrying capacities in arid interfluvial tracts balanced by intensive irrigated cultivation along river inundation belts [@green2019discoverin; @garciamolsosa2023reconstruc].

### Vakataka Vidarbha and Northern Deccan Sphere

The southern macro-province (777.163 km², 19,73%) covers 3.094 catalogued settlements across the northern Deccan plateau, primarily modern Vidarbha, Khandesh and northern Maharashtra, extending into the northern fringes of the Krishna-Godavari doab and peninsular trade corridors [@shaw2013archaeolog; @neill2020empires; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade]. Governed by the Vakatakas from capitals at Nandivardhana and Pravarapura, the region witnessed brilliant artistic and architectural patronal activity, epitomised by the rock-cut Buddhist chaityas and viharas at Ajanta during the reign of Harishena (c. 475AD to 500AD) [@shaw2013archaeolog]. Coastal and peninsular trading hubs including Kanchipuram, Badami, Paithan, Amaravati, Sopara and Kalliena linked the Deccan with maritime routes [@seland2014archaeolog; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade]. Provincial population increased from 5,72M in 319AD to 6,49M in 500AD and reached 7,04M by 750AD (9,06 persons per km²).

```{r tbl-subregions, results='asis'}
sub_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function (rk) {
  r <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  a <- as.numeric(r$area_km2)
  p_319 <- as.numeric(r$population[["319"]])
  p_400 <- as.numeric(r$population[["400"]])
  p_500 <- as.numeric(r$population[["500"]])
  p_600 <- as.numeric(r$population[["600"]])
  p_650 <- as.numeric(r$population[["650"]])
  p_750 <- as.numeric(r$population[["750"]])
  dens_750 <- p_750 / a
  data.frame(
    Region = clean_text(r$name),
    Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(a, 0L), " (", viscount_fmt_number(a / tot_area * 100, 1L), "%)"),
    P319AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_319),
    P400AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_400),
    P500AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_500),
    P600AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_600),
    P650AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_650),
    P750AD = viscount_fmt_pop(p_750),
    Density750 = viscount_fmt_number(dens_750, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sub <- do.call(rbind, sub_rows)
df_tot <- data.frame(
  Region = "Regional Total",
  Area = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(tot_area, 0L), " (100%)"),
  P319AD = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_319),
  P400AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["400"]]),
  P500AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["500"]]),
  P600AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["600"]]),
  P650AD = viscount_fmt_pop(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[["650"]]),
  P750AD = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_750),
  Density750 = viscount_fmt_number(tot_750 / tot_area, 2L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_sub <- rbind(df_sub, df_tot)
viscount_table(
  df_sub,
  "Sub-regional land area, benchmark population trajectories and 750AD population density across Classical South Asia.",
  c("Macro-Province", "Area km² (Share)", "319AD", "400AD", "500AD", "600AD", "650AD", "750AD", "750AD Density"),
  list(label = "tab:subregions", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Agrarian Expansion, Water Management and Land Grants

## Epigraphic Charters and Agrarian Colonisation

A central dynamic of the classical period was the systematic expansion of the agrarian frontier facilitated by royal land grants inscribed on copper plates (*tamra-shasana*) and stone stelae [@neill2020empires; @targa1999pala]. Rulers of the Gupta, Vakataka, Maitraka, Gauda and Kamarupa lineages granted uncultivated tracts (*khila*), forest margins (*aranya*) and entire revenue-bearing villages (*grama*) to learned Brahmins (*brahmadeya*), religious institutions (*devagrahara*) and Buddhist viharas [@shaw2013archaeolog; @dwivedi2021tools].

These charters conferred extensive fiscal immunities: exemption from regular royal taxes (*kara*, *bhaga* and *bhoga*), immunity from the entry of royal soldiers and revenue collectors (*a-chata-bhata-praveshya*), and rights to mineral, timber and water resources. In return, grant recipients served as agrarian pioneers, organising forest clearance, introducing calendar-based agricultural techniques and integrating indigenous tribal populations into caste-based agrarian structures [@neill2020empires; @kovacs2024bengal]. In Bengal, copper plates from Damodarpur, Baigram and Gunaighar document the purchase of fallow state land by private individuals for donation to religious establishments, revealing an active land market and community involvement in rural boundary demarcation [@kovacs2024bengal].

## Epigraphic Corpus and Territorial Demarcation

The epigraphic record of land transactions reveals a highly formalised administrative mechanism for agrarian registration and boundary demarcation across northern India [@neill2020empires; @targa1999pala]. In northern Bengal (Pundravardhana bhukti), the five famous Damodarpur copper plates, dating from the reigns of Kumaragupta I and Budhagupta, detail the operation of the district administrative board (*adhikarana*) headed by the district officer (*ayuktaka*) alongside the chief merchant (*nagara-shreshthin*), caravan leader (*sarthavaha*), chief artisan (*prathama-kulika*) and chief scribe (*prathama-kayastha*) [@kovacs2024bengal]. Private buyers petitioned the board to purchase uncultivated fallow land (*aprahata-khila*) at the customary rate of three dinaras per *kulyavapa* (a land measure based on seed sown) to endow religious institutions.

Similarly, the Baigram copper plate of 448AD records the purchase of state land by two Brahmin brothers for the maintenance of a temple of Govindasvamin, with village record-keepers (*pustapalas*) conducting physical boundary surveys before royal confirmation [@kovacs2024bengal]. The Gunaighar copper plate of Vainyagupta (507AD) in Samatata grants land to the Mahayana Buddhist Vaivartika Sangha, specifying precise boundary markers including river distributaries, marsh edges and drainage channels. In Vidarbha, the Poona copper plate of Prabhavatigupta and the Rithpur plates of the Vakataka queen Bhavattarika document the donation of entire agricultural villages in the Wardha valley, establishing institutional religious networks that anchored rural cultivation in the Deccan [@shaw2013archaeolog; @neill2020empires].

## Hydraulic Engineering, Tank Irrigation and Water Lifting

Sustaining high demographic densities required advanced hydraulic infrastructure to mitigate seasonal precipitation deficits [@singh2020hydrology; @shaw2003ancient]. Ancient Indian texts, including the *Brihat Samhita* of Varahamihira and the *Arthashastra* tradition, dedicate substantial treatises to water prospecting, reservoir siting and dam construction [@singh2020hydrology].

Archaeological excavations confirm the widespread construction of irrigation tanks (*tataka*), storage reservoirs (*vapi*) and stepped masonry wells across central and western India [@shaw2003ancient]. In Vidisha and Sanchi, Shaw and Sutcliffe documented an extensive network of ancient earthen dams and irrigation reservoirs dating to the early historic and classical periods, engineered to capture monsoon runoff from sandstone plateaux and release water through masonry sluices into surrounding agricultural plains [@shaw2003ancient]. In Saurashtra, the Junagadh inscription of Skandagupta records the breach of the monumental Sudarshana lake embankment during severe storms in 456AD and its restoration within two years by the provincial governor Parnadatta and his son Chakrapalita, who constructed a masonry dam one hundred cubits wide and forty cubits high [@singh2020hydrology].

Technological innovations in water lifting expanded irrigation beyond riverbanks. The *arahatta* or pot-garland wheel (*ghati-yantra*), rotated by bullock or manual labour, enabled continuous extraction of groundwater from deep masonry wells, permitting the cultivation of dry-season crops such as barley, wheat and sugarcane across northern India and Gujarat [@singh2020hydrology; @dwivedi2021tools].

## Monsoon Dynamics and Agrarian Resilience

High-resolution speleothem palaeoclimate records from Sahiya Cave and regional lake sediment cores indicate that the mid-first millennium AD experienced fluctuating Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) precipitation [@dixit2014abrupt; @rakesh2022ecological]. A stable and relatively humid climatic interval characterised the fourth and fifth centuries AD, supporting agricultural expansion across the northern river valleys [@jha2025geoarchaeo]. Towards the mid-sixth century AD, palaeoclimatic proxies record intervals of monsoon weakening, contemporaneous with global climate cooling linked to volcanic sulphate veils in 536AD and 540AD [@dixit2014abrupt; @islam2020late].

The diversification of cropping systems provided vital resilience against environmental volatility [@petrie2017adaptation; @singh2017counter]. Agrarian communities practiced multi-cropping regimes: deep-water winter rice (*aman*) and autumn rice (*aus*) in the humid Bengal delta, paired with *kharif* summer millets and *rabi* winter pulses, wheat and oilseeds across the drier western plains [@petrie2017adaptation; @kovacs2024bengal]. The extensive distribution of irrigation tanks and groundwater wells buffered crop production against delayed monsoon rains, preventing localized droughts from degenerating into regional famines.

## Agro-Ecological Zonation and Cropping Regimes

The diverse ecological zones of classical South Asia sustained highly specialised agricultural regimes matched to local soil and rainfall conditions [@singh2020hydrology; @petrie2017adaptation; @rakesh2022ecological]. In the lower Gangetic delta and coastal Bengal, the primary staple was deep-water transplanted winter rice (*shali*), supplemented by broadcast autumn rice (*vrihi*) and spring rice (*boro*) along river depressions [@kovacs2024bengal]. Classical agronomic treatises such as the *Krishi-Parashara* and the *Brihat Samhita* describe careful seed selection, organic manuring using cow dung and oilseed cake, and astrological calendar management for synchronising sowing with the onset of the *Rohini* and *Ardra* nakshatras [@singh2020hydrology].

Across the drier western and north-western doabs of Uttar Pradesh, Punjab and Sindh, agriculture was anchored in a dual-cropping cycle (*kharif* and *rabi*) [@petrie2017adaptation; @singh2017counter]. Summer monsoon crops included pearl millet (*bajra*), sorghum (*jowar*), sesamum (*tila*) and cotton (*karpasa*), while winter cultivation produced wheat (*godhuma*), barley (*yava*), chickpeas (*chanaka*), mustard (*sarshapa*) and lentils (*masura*). In Malwa and Gujarat, the moisture-retentive black-cotton soils (*regur*) supported extensive cotton and sugarcane (*ikshu*) plantations, providing high-value agricultural cash commodities that fueled textile manufacturing and long-distance caravan trade [@sheikh2004state; @dwivedi2021tools].

# Settlement Hierarchies and the Urban-Decline Debate

## Archaeology of Classical Urban Centres

Classical South Asia maintained an intricate settlement hierarchy ranging from imperial metropolises and provincial administrative capitals to fortified market towns (*nigama*), trading ports (*pattana*) and nucleated agrarian villages [@bettencourt2021introducti; @hawken2021long]. Archaeological mound surveys and remote sensing across northern and north-western India have identified thousands of settlement mounds (*tepe* or *theri*) displaying continuous occupational strata from the early historic through classical periods [@orengo2020automated; @green2019discoverin; @garciamolsosa2023reconstruc; @petrie2025hidden].

In Madhyadesha, major urban centres were characterised by monumental burnt-brick architecture, paved drainage conduits, domestic brick wells and extensive terracotta manufacturing [@khan2013bricks; @hawkes2020back; @Allchin1995Archaeology]. Pataliputra (Patna), though gradually yielding exclusive primacy as the northern imperial seat, remained the largest city of the fourth and fifth centuries, expanding from 145.000 inhabitants in 319AD to a peak of 175.000 in 400AD before receding to 140.000 in 500AD, 85.000 in 600AD and 45.000 by 750AD. Varanasi maintained steady demographic mass, advancing from 74.655 in 319AD to 81.425 in 500AD and peaking at 85.000 inhabitants in 600AD (retaining 80.000 in 750AD), while Mathura declined gently from its early classical peak of 76.175 in 319AD to 68.000 in 400AD and 46.784 by 750AD [@hawkes2020back; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation].

Kannauj (Kanyakubja) experienced dramatic demographic expansion as it evolved from a regional Gupta provincial headquarters into the imperial capital of the Maukhari and Pushyabhuti realms. Its population climbed from 39.950 in 319AD and 45.000 in 400AD to 70.356 in 500AD, 110.000 in 600AD and a peak of 140.000 inhabitants in 650AD (retaining 125.000 in 750AD) [@Chattopadhyaya1994Making; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation]. When the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited Kannauj in 636AD during Harsha's reign, he recorded a magnificent metropolis four miles long and one mile wide, enclosed by formidable defensive moats and high towers, housing one hundred Buddhist monasteries and more than two hundred Deva temples [@targa1999pala; @verardi2018gods].

In the north-west, Peshawar (Purushapura) stood at a peak of 70.703 inhabitants in 319AD (65.000 in 400AD) before contracting to 32.000 by 650AD, while Taxila fell from 53.190 in 319AD and 45.000 in 400AD to 12.000 in 500AD following Huna disruptions [@khattak2025major; @morris2019central]. Over the same centuries, Thanesar expanded to 55.000 inhabitants in 600AD, Multan rose to 52.139 by 750AD, and both Srinagar and Delhi reached 48.000 by 750AD. In western India, Ujjain peaked at 95.000 inhabitants in 400AD (90.693 in 319AD, 86.081 in 500AD), integrating overland routes from the Gangetic valley with the coastal ports of Gujarat, while Valabhi expanded from 25.000 in 500AD to a peak of 65.000 in 650AD as the political and scholastic capital of the Maitrakas [@sheikh2004state; @verardi2018gods]. In the south, Kanchipuram rose steadily from 43.667 in 319AD to 60.000 in 500AD and peaked at 85.000 inhabitants in 650AD [@Champakalakshmi1996Trade].

## Structural Evolution of Excavated Gangetic Cities

Systematic excavations across the Gangetic basin illuminate the material reality of urban transformations between the fourth and eighth centuries AD [@hawkes2020back; @khan2013bricks]. At Ahichchhatra in Bareilly district, extensive stratigraphy demonstrates the construction of massive tiered brick temples (notably Temple AC II) dedicated to Shiva, alongside magnificent terracotta sculptures depicting the river goddesses Ganga and Yamuna dating to the Gupta period [@hawkes2020back]. Although residential density within the fortified enclosure reorganised in the post-Gupta era, religious monumentalism and surrounding settlement mounds persisted through the eighth century AD.

At Kaushambi, excavations around the Ghoshitarama monastery and royal palace complex demonstrate substantial structural rebuilding under the Guptas, followed by evidence of destruction attributed to the Hunas under Toramana [@hawkes2020back; @morris2019central]. Nevertheless, occupation continued across peripheral mounds. At Rajghat (ancient Varanasi), excavations revealed continuous structural phases characterised by fired-brick dwellings, public drainage systems, sealings and terracotta figurines spanning the entire first millennium AD without systemic occupational hiatus [@hawkes2020back]. In Bengal, excavations at Rajbadidanga in Murshidabad district confirmed the identification of Karnasuvarna, the seventh-century capital of Shashanka, revealing extensive monastic and residential foundations that flourished alongside deltaic agrarian colonisation [@kovacs2024bengal; @targa1999pala].

## Re-evaluating Urban Decay and Ruralisation

A prominent historiographical debate has centred on the degree of urban vitality during the post-Gupta era. Historians associated with the Indian feudalism thesis posited a widespread urban decay (*shahar hras*) between 300AD and 1000AD, arguing that the decline of long-distance Roman commerce, coin shortages and the proliferation of land grants led to de-urbanisation, economic self-sufficiency and the ruralisation of society [@dwivedi2021tools; @seland2014archaeolog].

Recent archaeological syntheses and field surveys challenge this monolithic model [@Chattopadhyaya1994Making; @hawkes2020back; @garciamolsosa2023reconstruc; @petrie2025hidden]. While certain early historic cities in the middle Gangetic valley (such as Kaushambi, Shravasti and Rajgir) experienced physical contraction or structural reorganisation in their core monumental zones, this process was accompanied by the simultaneous emergence and expansion of new regional urban nodes [@hawkes2020back; @bettencourt2021introducti; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation]. Settlement shifted towards regional political centres like Kannauj, Valabhi, Kanchipuram, Karnasuvarna and Gaur, as well as rural market centres and temple complexes that stimulated local exchange networks [@targa1999pala; @kovacs2024bengal; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade]. Far from demonstrating aggregate demographic decline, the archaeological record demonstrates a redistribution of urban populations across a more decentralised, polycentric regional network [@hawken2021long; @bettencourt2021introducti; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making].

Epigraphic records from western and central India further demonstrate the vitality of inter-regional merchants and itinerant traders (*sarthavahas*) during the post-Gupta centuries [@dwivedi2021tools; @sheikh2004state]. Inscriptions from Gwalior, Kota and Kaman record gifts by merchant corporations and oil-millers to local sanctuaries, confirming that capital accumulation continued outside imperial capitals [@neill2020empires]. Moreover, the continuity of craft specialization across early mediaeval temple towns indicates that urbanization in South Asia followed a polycentric evolutionary trajectory rather than a unilinear boom-and-bust cycle [@hawkes2020back; @bettencourt2021introducti]. As regional administrative seats took root in Bengal, Gujarat and the Deccan, commercial exchange reorganized around local agricultural hinterlands, ensuring resilient economic integration across changing political regimes [@targa1999pala; @kovacs2024bengal].

## Monastic Complexes and Knowledge Networks

Buddhist Mahaviharas and Brahmanical temple complexes played a structural role in regional demographic and economic organization [@shaw2013archaeolog; @verardi2018gods; @morris2021economic]. Monasteries were not isolated ascetic retreats, but major landholders, consumers of agricultural surplus and centres of manufacturing and literacy. Nalanda, established in the fifth century AD under Kumaragupta I, expanded into a sprawling monastic university that housed several thousand resident scholar-monks, supported by revenues from more than two hundred endowed villages [@shaw2013archaeolog; @verardi2018gods].

Monastic establishments in Saurashtra, notably at Valabhi, received extensive endowments from Maitraka rulers, serving as centres of intellectual exchange and international pilgrimage frequented by Chinese scholars such as Yijing [@sheikh2004state; @verardi2018gods]. In eastern India, monastic centres at Paharpur (Somapura) and Mainamati (Salban Vihara) anchored rural colonization in the Bengal delta, functioning as nodes of literacy, legal administration and technological dissemination [@targa1999pala; @kovacs2024bengal].

## Guild Organisations and Artisan Production

A defining feature of classical urban economies was the institutional organisation of craftspeople and merchants into autonomous guilds (*shreni*, *nigama* and *puga*) [@dwivedi2021tools; @neill2020empires]. Epigraphic records and clay sealings discovered at Bhita, Basarh (ancient Vaishali), Rajghat and Nalanda attest to corporate bodies of oil-millers (*tailika-shreni*), potters (*kumbhakara*), weavers (*tantuvaya*), metalworkers and ivory-carvers operating under their own customary laws (*shreni-dharma*) recognized by imperial courts [@hawkes2020back; @khattak2025major].

These guilds performed sophisticated commercial and banking functions, receiving perpetual cash endowments (*akshaya-nivi*) from royals and wealthy citizens, paying regular interest to fund daily lamps in temples or food for Buddhist monks [@shaw2013archaeolog; @verardi2018gods]. The celebrated fifth-century Mandasor stone inscription of Kumaragupta I and Bandhuvarman records that a guild of silk-weavers (*pattavaya*) migrated from Lata (southern Gujarat) to Dashapura (Mandasor in western Malwa), attracted by the enlightened patronage of the local ruler, and pooled their collective resources to construct and later renovate a magnificent sun temple [@sheikh2004state; @dwivedi2021tools]. Such collective civic agency proves that urban artisan communities remained active and resilient corporate institutions throughout the classical period.

## Maritime Commerce and Trade Corridors

Although western trade with the Roman Empire evolved following the crisis of the third century AD, maritime connectivity in the Indian Ocean remained robust [@seland2014archaeolog; @cobb2018black]. Sasanian Persia and the Byzantine Empire maintained active commercial exchanges with western Indian ports. Ports along the Gulf of Khambhat and Saurashtra, including Bharuch (39.070 peak in 319AD), Cambay and Sopara (23.480 peak in 319AD), exported cotton textiles, indigo, fine ceramics, iron and semi-precious stones to Persian Gulf and Red Sea destinations [@seland2014archaeolog; @dwivedi2021tools].

In the Bay of Bengal, maritime routes expanded dramatically between eastern India and Southeast Asia. Tamralipti (38.000 peak in 400AD) in the Ganges delta served as the premier international port for maritime voyages to Sri Lanka, Java, Sumatra and China [@kovacs2024bengal]. Chinese pilgrims Faxian (in 411AD) and Xuanzang (in 637AD) both embarked from Tamralipti on their homeward voyages. The circulation of cowrie shells as everyday currency alongside gold dinaras and silver drammas facilitated both local village transactions and international maritime trade [@dwivedi2021tools; @sheikh2004state].

The *Christian Topography* of Cosmas Indicopleustes, composed around 550AD, confirms that ports such as Kalyan, Chaul and Bharuch handled heavy maritime freight, exchanging pepper, silk and aromatics between South Asia, Ceylon, Sasanian Persia and the Mediterranean [@seland2014archaeolog; @cobb2018black]. Furthermore, coastal communities constructed stone-anchored jetties and beacon installations along the Kathiawar peninsula to facilitate navigation across seasonal cyclone tracks [@sheikh2004state; @kumar2025investigat].

# Methodological Framework and Spatial Calibration

## Spatial Engine and Environmental Covariates

To distribute population across the 3.938.787 km² domain, the INDUS spatial engine models 51.246 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells. Each grid cell is evaluated using biophysical and accessibility covariates:
- Fluvial distance decay: proximity to major perennial river channels (Ganga, Yamuna, Brahmaputra, Indus, Narmada, Tapti, Godavari and Krishna), applying exponential density attenuation beyond 25 km from navigable waterways.
- Topographic wetness and terrain slope: penalising steep Himalayan and Western Ghat scarps while favouring flat alluvial terraces and fertile volcanic plateaux.
- Monsoon precipitation and agricultural suitability: incorporating regional rainfall isohyets, soil water storage capacity and multi-cropping potential [@singh2020hydrology; @petrie2017adaptation].
- Archaeological mound and site density: incorporating surveyed site clusters identified through remote sensing and historical survey records [@orengo2020automated; @green2019discoverin; @petrie2025hidden].

## Settlement Subtraction and Rural Allocation

To isolate nucleated urban populations from rural agriculturalists, 12.898 catalogued settlements with chronological population series are georeferenced to their exact WGS84 coordinates (2.484 in Madhyadesha and Magadha, 2.744 in Gauda, Bengal and Kamarupa, 2.165 in Malwa and Gujarat, 2.411 in Punjab, Kashmir and Sindh, and 3.094 in the Vakataka Deccan). The expanded gazetteer draws on primary-monograph historical metropolis reconstructions [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation; @Hambly1982Towns], multi-repository archaeological and monument corpora, official national census tables and pre-1800 *qasba*, *pargana* and *nadu* continuity [@Habib1982Atlas; @Moosvi1987Economy; @Bayly1983Rulers; @ImperialGazetteer1908], yielding a Zipf rank-size slope of $\alpha = 0,87$ ($R^2 = 0,96$). At each benchmark year, the active population of catalogued settlements within each macro-province is aggregated and subtracted from the provincial demographic envelope.

The residual rural population is then allocated across non-settled pixels in proportion to the calibrated environmental suitability index. A two-pass boundary smoothing filter ensures continuous demographic gradients across provincial frontiers, preventing artificial density cliffs along administrative borders.

## Uncertainty Envelopes and Demographic Bounds

Every provincial and regional benchmark estimate incorporates an explicit symmetric uncertainty bound (+/- 23% across all benchmark years from 319AD to 750AD). In 500AD, the macro-regional total of 59,00M is bounded between 45,43M and 72,57M inhabitants. This uncertainty envelope accommodates historical variance in household size multipliers, urban density assumptions and epigraphic land measurement interpretations.

## Long-Term Population Benchmarks

The demographic history of classical South Asia across four centuries reveals steady, sustainable expansion anchored in rural agricultural colonization and regional urban adaptation (Figure \ref{fig:trajectory} and Table \ref{tab:benchmarks}).

```{r tbl-benchmarks, results='asis'}
bm_years <- c("319", "400", "500", "600", "650", "750")
bm_rows <- lapply(bm_years, function (yk) {
  tot_pop <- as.numeric(mod_data$summary$headline_population_by_benchmark[[yk]])
  mad <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$gup_madhyadesha_magadha$population[[yk]])
  gau <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$gup_gauda_vanga_kamarupa$population[[yk]])
  mal <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$gup_malwa_gujarat_saurashtra$population[[yk]])
  pun <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$gup_punjab_kashmir_sindh$population[[yk]])
  vak <- as.numeric(mod_data$regions$gup_vakataka_deccan$population[[yk]])
  dens <- tot_pop / tot_area
  data.frame(
    Benchmark = fmt_yr(yk),
    TotalPop = viscount_fmt_pop(tot_pop),
    Density = viscount_fmt_number(dens, 2L),
    Madhyadesha = viscount_fmt_pop(mad),
    GaudaBengal = viscount_fmt_pop(gau),
    MalwaGujarat = viscount_fmt_pop(mal),
    PunjabNorthWest = viscount_fmt_pop(pun),
    VakatakaDeccan = viscount_fmt_pop(vak),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_bm <- do.call(rbind, bm_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_bm,
  "Benchmark population totals and provincial distribution across Classical South Asia (319AD to 750AD).",
  c("Benchmark", "Regional Pop", "Density km²", "Madhyadesha", "Gauda-Bengal", "Malwa-Gujarat", "Punjab-NW", "Deccan"),
  list(label = "tab:benchmarks", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

## Chronological Demographic Trajectories

### Early Gupta Rise and Consolidation (319AD to 400AD)

Between the founding of the Gupta era in 319AD and the closing years of Chandragupta II's reign around 400AD, the subcontinent experienced steady demographic expansion under unified imperial administration [@neill2020empires]. Regional population grew from 52,00M in 319AD to 56,50M in 400AD (+8,65%), reflecting an annual growth rate of 0,10%.

During this phase, political stability eliminated internal transit tariffs across northern India, stimulating artisan production and inter-regional grain transport [@dwivedi2021tools]. The Madhyadesha core expanded from 17,68M to 19,21M inhabitants, while Gauda and Bengal rose from 11,44M to 12,43M. When the Chinese pilgrim Faxian travelled across northern India between 399AD and 412AD, he described Madhyadesha as a prosperous, peaceful country where the people were numerous and happy, free from oppressive corporal punishments or transit registries [@hawkes2020back].

### Classical Zenith and Imperial Apex (400AD to 500AD)

The fifth century AD represented the imperial zenith of classical Indian civilization [@neill2020empires; @shaw2013archaeolog]. Regional population advanced from 56,50M in 400AD to 59,00M in 500AD (+4,42%), achieving an aggregate density of 14,98 persons per km².

Under Kumaragupta I and Skandagupta, state resources supported monumental architecture, irrigation maintenance and academic institutions. Agricultural colonisation extended into the forested tracts of central India and the deltaic islands of Bengal [@kovacs2024bengal]. Major imperial centres reached substantial demographic scales during this interval: Patna peaked at 175.000 inhabitants in 400AD (standing at 140.000 in 500AD), Ujjain peaked at 95.000 in 400AD (86.081 in 500AD), Varanasi expanded from 78.000 to 81.425, Mathura stood at 68.000 in 400AD (61.156 in 500AD), and Kanchipuram rose from 48.000 to 60.000.

### Huna Incursions and Regional Fragmentation (500AD to 600AD)

The sixth century AD brought major geopolitical transformations. Incursions by the Hunas fractured imperial authority in Punjab and the north-west, sacking cities such as Taxila (which contracted from 45.000 in 400AD to 12.000 in 500AD) and disrupting trans-Eurasian trade routes [@morris2019central; @verardi2012buddhism]. In the imperial core, succession disputes weakened the Later Guptas, while regional feudatories declared independence.

Despite political decentralisation, demographic momentum continued, driven by expanding rural agriculture and local land grants [@targa1999pala; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making]. Regional population grew from 59,00M in 500AD to 61,00M in 600AD (+3,39%). Growth shifted towards emerging regional capitals: Kannauj grew from 70.356 to 110.000, Varanasi peaked at 85.000, Thanesar rose from 35.000 to 55.000, and Valabhi expanded from 25.000 to 55.000 as Maitraka rulers established autonomous commercial jurisdiction across Gujarat [@sheikh2004state].

### Harsha of Kannauj and the Post-Gupta Re-alignment (600AD to 650AD)

The first half of the seventh century AD was dominated by Harshavardhana of Kannauj (606AD to 647AD), who reunited northern India from Punjab to the borders of Bengal and the Narmada [@targa1999pala; @verardi2018gods]. Harsha established Kannauj as the premier metropolis of northern India, where the city reached its peak of 140.000 inhabitants in 650AD, documented in detail by Banabhatta in the *Harshacharita* and by Xuanzang in his *Si-Yu-Ki*.

Subcontinental population expanded from 61,00M in 600AD to 62,50M in 650AD (+2,46%). Xuanzang travelled extensively throughout the subcontinent, describing teeming rural populations, flourishing orchards and fertile grain fields, alongside flourishing monastic and royal establishments in Nalanda (25.000 peak in 650AD), Valabhi (65.000 peak in 650AD) and Kanchipuram (85.000 peak in 650AD) [@shaw2013archaeolog; @verardi2018gods; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade].

### Pre-Mediaeval Equilibrium (650AD to 750AD)

Following Harsha's death in 647AD, northern India entered an era of tri-partite regional competition involving the Later Guptas of Magadha, the rising Gurjara-Pratiharas of Rajasthan, the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan and the Palas of Bengal [@targa1999pala; @kovacs2024bengal]. Regional population reached 64,00M by 750AD (+2,40% over 650AD), yielding an aggregate density of 16,25 persons per km².

In eastern India, the foundation of the Pala dynasty under Gopala around 750AD brought stability to Bengal, establishing Gaur (Lakshmanavati) as a premier regional capital supporting 65.000 inhabitants alongside Mahasthangarh (41.352 in 750AD). In Gujarat, Patan (Anhilwara) emerged at 20.000 inhabitants alongside Valabhi (55.000) and Bharuch (37.118), while Multan (52.139), Srinagar (48.000) and Delhi (48.000) anchored the north-west. The decentralised agrarian economy established during the Gupta era matured into the regional kingdoms of the early mediaeval period.

# Leading Settlements and Urban Clusters

The INDUS gazetteer integrates 12.898 catalogued classical settlements across South Asia ($\alpha = 0,87$, $R^2 = 0,96$), reconciling primary-monograph urban reconstructions, archaeological mound surveys, epigraphic toponyms, official census baselines and historical accounts [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making; @ImperialGazetteer1908]. Table \ref{tab:leading_settlements} presents the leading settlements across the five macro-provinces, illustrating their demographic peaks and chronological trajectories.

```{r tbl-leading-settlements, results='asis'}
set_list <- unname(set_data)
sett_peaks <- vapply(set_list, function (s) {
  if (is.null(s$population) || length(s$population) == 0) return(0)
  max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
}, numeric(1))

ord <- order(sett_peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_sett <- set_list[ord]

top_rows <- lapply(head(top_sett, 15), function (s) {
  p_max <- max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
  p_500 <- if (!is.null(s$population[["500"]])) as.numeric(s$population[["500"]]) else "-"
  p_750 <- if (!is.null(s$population[["750"]])) as.numeric(s$population[["750"]]) else "-"
  lat <- as.numeric(s$coords[[1]])
  lon <- as.numeric(s$coords[[2]])
  coord_str <- paste0(viscount_fmt_number(abs(lat), 2L), if (lat >= 0) " N" else " S", ", ",
                      viscount_fmt_number(abs(lon), 2L), if (lon >= 0) " E" else " W")
  data.frame(
    Name = clean_text(s$name),
    MacroProvince = clean_text(s$region),
    Coordinates = coord_str,
    PeakPop = viscount_fmt_pop(p_max),
    P500AD = if (is.numeric(p_500)) viscount_fmt_pop(p_500) else "-",
    P750AD = if (is.numeric(p_750)) viscount_fmt_pop(p_750) else "-",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_top <- do.call(rbind, top_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_top,
  "Leading classical settlements across South Asia, showing coordinates, peak population, and 500AD and 750AD benchmarks.",
  c("Settlement Name", "Macro-Province", "Coordinates", "Peak Pop", "500AD Pop", "750AD Pop"),
  list(label = "tab:leading_settlements", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

The urban hierarchy of classical South Asia was headed by Patna (Pataliputra) in the Madhyadesha core, which peaked at 175.000 inhabitants in 400AD (140.000 in 500AD, receding to 45.000 in 750AD), followed by Kannauj (Kanyakubja), which expanded to 140.000 inhabitants in 650AD under Harsha and maintained 125.000 in 750AD [@Allchin1995Archaeology; @hawkes2020back; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making]. Ujjain in Malwa peaked at 95.000 inhabitants in 400AD (71.836 in 750AD), while Varanasi peaked at 85.000 in 600AD (80.000 in 750AD) and Kanchipuram in the southern sphere reached 85.000 in 650AD (82.128 in 750AD) [@sheikh2004state; @Champakalakshmi1996Trade]. Rounding out the top eight classical centres were Mathura (76.175 peak in 319AD), Peshawar (70.703 peak in 319AD) and Valabhi (65.000 peak in 650AD) [@khattak2025major; @verardi2018gods].

Among secondary provincial capitals, Gaur expanded to 65.000 inhabitants by 750AD under early Pala rule, Thanesar peaked at 55.000 in 600AD, Taxila stood at 53.190 in 319AD before fifth-century contraction, Multan reached 52.139 in 750AD, Badami peaked at 52.000 in 650AD, Ayodhya peaked at 52.000 in 400AD, and both Srinagar and Delhi reached 48.000 in 750AD [@kovacs2024bengal; @targa1999pala; @morris2019central]. By coupling these 12.898 georeferenced settlement trajectories with spatial kriging and environmental suitability covariates, INDUS isolates nucleated urban populations while allocating rural agricultural inhabitants across the non-settled landscape.
